**The Clockwork Kitchen** ⭐⭐⭐⭐ (4/5)

Tucked away in a converted Victorian boiler house on the edge of the Arts District, The Clockwork Kitchen delivers exactly the kind of theatrical dining experience its brass-and-gears aesthetic promises—and occasionally threatens to overwhelm.

First impressions are stunning. The dining room is a cathedral of copper piping, exposed brick, and gently rotating kinetic sculptures that cast dancing shadows across the mahogany tables. It’s immersive without feeling like a theme park, though the ambient ticking of two dozen mechanical clocks takes some getting used to. By dessert, I found it either meditative or maddening—your mileage may vary.

Chef Amara Voss’s menu describes itself as “Neo-Industrial Comfort Food,” which turns out to be code for beautifully reimagined classics with unexpected mechanical twists. The “Pressure-Valve” pork belly appetizer (£14) arrived under a glass cloche filled with applewood smoke that released in a dramatic hiss when lifted. The meat itself was flawless: 36-hour sous vide rendered the fat silky and translucent, paired with a sharp pickled fennel that cut through the richness. Less successful was the “Gearbox” bread service—sourdough baked in custom springform pans to resemble cogs. Novel? Absolutely. But the dense, under-seasoned crumb felt like form sacrificed too much for function.

Mains soared. My “Steam Engine” seafood risotto (£26) was genuinely exceptional, served in a miniature copper cauldron over a controlled flame that kept the Arborio at the perfect temperature. The saffron broth was deeply layered, and the charred octopus tentacle curling over the top had a smoky, caramelized crust that made me close my eyes on the first bite. My companion’s venison loin, plated with a beetroot “oil slick” and aerated bone-marrow foam, was similarly ambitious and largely successful, though the foam dissolved too quickly to contribute much beyond Instagram appeal.

Service struck the right balance of knowledgeable and playful. Our server, dressed in a waistcoat and goggles (resting on his forehead, never ostentatiously worn), explained the cocktail list with genuine passion. The “Tesla Coil” old fashioned—smoked tableside with an actual handheld electric coil—was delicious, if slightly terrifying.

The 15% automatic service charge felt steep given that water refills were slow during a busy Friday service, and at £140 for two (with wine), The Clockwork Kitchen sits firmly in special-occasion territory. But when the kitchen isn’t distracted by its own gimmicks, the food is undeniably skilled.

**Verdict:** Come for the spectacle, stay for the pork belly and risotto. Just don’t expect to have a quiet conversation—or check the time.
